# Quiet Library

Quiet Library is a personal, distraction-free YouTube video library for Android. It stores only videos you deliberately save, organizes them into local folders, and plays a selected video in a constrained embedded player without exposing search, comments, Shorts, trending pages, or a general YouTube feed.

The app targets Expo SDK 57, React Native 0.86, TypeScript, Android 14+, and the Samsung Galaxy A15.

## What is implemented

- Paste standard, short, mobile, music, live, embed, or Shorts-form YouTube video URLs.
- Validate links, reject unsupported URLs, and prevent duplicate saved videos.
- Load title, thumbnail, and channel through YouTube oEmbed without an API key.
- Enrich duration, publication date, and description through YouTube Data API v3 when a key is configured.
- Store saved videos, metadata, folders, assignments, and local-availability state in SQLite.
- Create, rename, and delete folders; move videos between folders; view all or unfiled videos.
- Select multiple saved videos, including all videos in the current view, then move or delete them together.
- Show each saved video's local availability and the queued, transferring, completed, failed, or interrupted transfer state.
- Keep videos when deleting a folder by default, with a separate explicit destructive option.
- Present source-controlled channels as folder-like entries, with separate paginated Videos and Playlists views.
- Load additional channel, playlist, and playlist-video pages automatically near the end of each list while caching channel videos locally.
- Register separate Android URL intent filters for `youtu.be`, `/watch`, `/shorts`, and `/live` links so supported links can open directly in Quiet Library from the system chooser.
- Play only the selected video in an embedded YouTube player, block top-level YouTube navigation, and replace the player with a native replay panel at playback end instead of leaving recommendations visible.
- Offer **Save video** in the player when a link opened from another Android app is not yet in the library.
- Use a dark, low-glare interface throughout the app.
- Show explicit loading, empty, invalid-link, API, and playback states.
- Use disk-backed thumbnail caching and virtualized lists for low memory use.

## Local availability state

Each saved video has an **Offline availability** sheet. SQLite stores its transfer state, progress, and completed local file URI. The supported states are `unavailable`, `queued`, `downloading`, `downloaded`, `failed`, and `interrupted`.

This release provides the storage model and status UI. It does not include a file-transfer backend; a configured transfer service can update those fields and the sheet will reflect its progress and result.

## Architecture and storage

The app intentionally avoids a large state-management or navigation dependency.

- `LibraryProvider` is the single application-state boundary. It coordinates repository operations, YouTube metadata, cached channel feeds, and refresh state.
- `NavigationProvider` is a small stack navigator with Android hardware-back handling.
- `expo-sqlite` stores relational local data in `quiet-library.db`. SQLite is a better fit than one large JSON value because uniqueness, folder relationships, transactions, and future migrations remain explicit and reliable. WAL mode keeps reads responsive while writes occur.
- `expo-image` uses memory-and-disk caching for thumbnails. Images are not copied into SQLite.
- `react-native-webview` hosts the supported YouTube IFrame Player. The containing document uses the Android application ID as its HTTPS origin so YouTube receives app identity/referrer information.
- No background polling or background tasks are registered.

The SQLite schema is created in [`src/data/database.ts`](src/data/database.ts). Deleting the Android app also deletes its private database and cached thumbnails.

├── App.tsx
├── app.config.ts
├── eas.json
├── package.json
├── tsconfig.json
├── .env.example
├── assets
│   ├── icon.svg / icon.png
│   └── adaptive-icon.svg / adaptive-icon.png
└── src
    ├── components

Downloads are handled by the companion server in [`server/`](server): the app posts a video id, the server prepares an MP4 with yt-dlp + FFmpeg, and the app then transfers the finished file into its private storage with `expo-file-system`, updating status and progress in SQLite along the way.

### Download server

```bash
cd server
npm install
npm start   # listens on port 3000 (override with PORT)
```

The machine running the server needs [`yt-dlp`](https://github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp) and [`ffmpeg`](https://ffmpeg.org/) on its `PATH` (or set `YT_DLP_PATH`). Point the app at it with `EXPO_PUBLIC_DOWNLOAD_SERVER_URL` in `.env` (for example `http://192.168.1.10:3000` when the phone and server share a network). When the variable is unset the Offline availability sheet explains how to enable downloads instead of showing the download button. Downloads that were in flight when the app closed are marked `interrupted` on the next launch and can be retried; deleting a saved video also deletes its local file. Only download videos you have the right to save offline.

The download feature is done, fully on-device — no backend needed. Typecheck passes, and I verified the whole pipeline live from this machine: YouTube's player API returns an OK playability status, the app picks the itag 18 progressive MP4 (360p, muxed audio+video so no FFmpeg is required), and the returned URL serves real MP4 bytes.

How it works:

- **`src/services/downloads.ts`** (new) — resolves a direct stream URL by calling YouTube's internal player API with the `ANDROID_VR` client (this client returns plain, unciphered URLs), then downloads the file to the app's private storage (`downloads/<videoId>.mp4`) using `expo-file-system` with byte-level progress callbacks. It also handles unplayable videos (private, age-restricted, region-locked) by surfacing YouTube's reason in the error.
- **`LibraryContext`** — new `downloadVideo` and `removeDownload` functions. Progress updates patch React state on every callback but only write to SQLite every 5% to avoid write churn. Concurrent duplicate downloads are prevented, downloads left in `queued`/`downloading` when the app closes are marked `interrupted` on next launch, and deleting a saved video (single or bulk) also deletes its local file.
- **`repository.ts`** — added `updateDownloadState` and `markStaleDownloadsInterrupted` for the existing `download_status` / `download_progress` / `downloaded_file_uri` columns (no schema change needed).
- **Offline availability sheet** — now shows a **Download video** button (or **Retry download** after a failure/interruption), a disabled "Transfer in progress" state with the existing live percentage, and **Remove local copy** once downloaded. The sheet reads the live video from context, so progress updates while it's open. Failures pop an alert with the reason.
- Installed `expo-file-system`; reverted the earlier backend-related changes (server folder, `.env` variable, cleartext-traffic plugin) after you said everything should run locally. README updated to describe the on-device flow and its limitations — the build/ADB instructions from your spec were already in the README.

Two notes: progressive streams top out at 360p (sometimes 720p) — higher resolutions only exist as separate audio/video streams, which would need on-device merging. And the player still streams via the YouTube embed; playing the downloaded file offline would need a native video player (`expo-video`) — say the word if you want that wired up next. Also, `App.tsx` shows as modified in git but that change predates my work; I didn't touch it.

It was a public client identifier hardcoded in YouTube's own apps that tools like yt-dlp used to send with every request. YouTube stopped requiring it a while back (which is why yt-dlp works without any key on the command line), and my test just confirmed the `ANDROID_VR` client works fine without it — the request is authenticated purely by the client name/version headers and body, same as before.

So downloads now work with zero keys and zero configuration. Note this is separate from the optional `EXPO_PUBLIC_YOUTUBE_API_KEY` in `.env`, which is still used only for metadata enrichment (durations, publish dates, channel feeds) — that one was already optional and is unrelated to downloading.

message.content: where is yt dlp and ffmpeg used?

content.text:
They aren't used anywhere anymore. That was the first iteration: your original paste described a backend server running yt-dlp + FFmpeg, so I built one in `server/`. When you then said everything should happen locally on the phone, I deleted that folder entirely and replaced the approach.

The current flow has no external tools at all:

1. **Stream resolution** — `resolveStreamUrl()` in `src/services/downloads.ts` does what yt-dlp's extractor does internally: it POSTs to YouTube's player API as the `ANDROID_VR` client and picks the best progressive MP4 format from the response.
2. **No FFmpeg needed** — FFmpeg was only ever required to merge separate audio and video streams. Progressive formats (itag 18) already contain both muxed together, so the file is playable as-is.
3. **File transfer** — `downloadToDevice()` streams the MP4 straight into app storage with `expo-file-system`.

The trade-off of skipping FFmpeg is the 360p cap I mentioned — higher resolutions only exist as separate audio/video streams that would need merging. If you ever want 720p+, that's when something like FFmpeg (or an on-device muxing library) would come back into the picture.

message.content: Would utube know about this?

content.text:
In the sense of "do the requests hit YouTube's servers" — yes, unavoidably. Every download makes two requests to Google infrastructure: one to the player API to resolve the stream URL, and one to `googlevideo.com` to fetch the file. YouTube sees your IP address, the video ID, and a client fingerprint claiming to be the YouTube VR app.

What they *don't* see:

- **Your identity.** The app sends no cookies, no login, no Google account — the requests are anonymous apart from your IP. This is unlike the YouTube API key in `.env`, which *is* tied to your Google Cloud account (but is only used for metadata, never for downloads).
- **Anything on your device.** Once the file is downloaded, playing it, keeping it, or deleting it is invisible to them.

Practical implications:

- **This is the same visibility yt-dlp has.** When you run yt-dlp from the command line, YouTube sees exactly the same kind of traffic. Millions of people do this; for personal, low-volume use it's background noise to them.
- **The realistic risk isn't punishment, it's breakage.** YouTube periodically tightens these internal APIs (the plain `ANDROID` client already stopped working, which is why we use `ANDROID_VR`). One day this client may also require extra tokens, and downloads will start failing until the app is updated — the same maintenance treadmill yt-dlp lives on.
- **Heavy volume from one IP can trigger rate-limiting** (HTTP 429s or throttled speeds). For a personal library of hand-picked videos you won't get near that.

One honest caveat: downloading outside the official app is against YouTube's Terms of Service regardless of tool. For personal offline viewing of content you have rights to, enforcement against individual users is essentially unheard of — but that's the formal position, and it's the same one that applies to yt-dlp itself.

## Build an installable APK locally

Generate the Android project and assemble a release APK:

```powershell
npx expo prebuild --platform android --clean
$env:NODE_ENV = 'production'
.\android\gradlew.bat -p android assembleRelease -PreactNativeArchitectures=arm64-v8a
```

Output:

```text
android/app/build/outputs/apk/release/app-release.apk
```

The generated local release uses the Expo template's development signing configuration and is suitable for direct device testing, not Play Store distribution. Create and protect a production keystore before publishing.

## Build an APK with EAS

The `preview` profile in `eas.json` is configured for an internally distributed APK:

```powershell
npx eas-cli login
npx eas-cli build --platform android --profile preview
```

For Play Store submission, use the `production` profile, which produces an Android App Bundle by default:

```powershell
npx eas-cli build --platform android --profile production
```

- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.text:
The "sign in to confirm you're not a bot" wall means YouTube is gating the bare InnerTube call from your IP. The NewPipe approach is the right fix: NewPipe Extractor is a battle-tested Java library that handles all the client rotation and token logic, and since this is an Android app we can embed it directly as a native Expo module (yt-dlp is Python, so it can't run inside the app). Downloading itself stays exactly as it is — only stream-URL resolution moves to the native library.

Done — the app is built, installed, and running on your Galaxy (`R58X30XXN6F`).

What changed for the NewPipe approach:

- **`modules/newpipe/`** — a local Expo native module (Kotlin) embedding **NewPipe Extractor v0.26.3** straight from TeamNewPipe's repo via JitPack. It exposes one function, `resolveStream(videoId)`, which runs the extractor's full YouTube logic (client selection, anti-bot handling — the part that was triggering the "sign in" wall) and returns the best progressive MP4 URL. An OkHttp-based downloader backs the extractor, matching how the NewPipe app itself wires it.
- **`src/services/downloads.ts`** — stream resolution now calls the native module instead of hitting YouTube's API from JavaScript. The file transfer, progress tracking, and SQLite state handling are unchanged. yt-dlp wasn't an option here since it's Python and can't run inside an Android app — NewPipe Extractor is the Java-native equivalent.
- The release APK (32 MB) built successfully in under 2 minutes, installed via `adb install -r`, and launched with a clean logcat — no crashes.

One caveat: since the extractor is a native library, downloads only work in real builds like this one, not in Expo Go (noted in the README).

The one thing I couldn't verify end-to-end is an actual download on the device, since that needs a tap in the UI. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates, layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.
- web-access: 所有联网操作必须通过此 skill 处理，包括：搜索、网页抓取、登录后操作、网络交互等。 触发场景：用户要求搜索信息、查看网页内容、访问需要登录的网站、操作网页界面、抓取社交媒体内容（小红书、微博、推特等）、读取动态渲染页面、以及任何需要真实浏览器环境的网络任务。
- feature-dev:feature-dev: Guided feature development with codebase understanding and architecture focus
- Notion:create-database-row: Insert a new row into a specified Notion database using natural-language property values.
- Notion:create-page: Create a new Notion page, optionally under a specific parent, using the Notion Workspace Skill and Notion MCP server.
- Notion:create-task: Create a new task in the user’s Notion tasks database with sensible defaults.
- Notion:database-query: Query a Notion database by name or ID and return structured, readable results.
- Notion:find: Quickly find pages or databases in Notion by title keywords.
- Notion:search: Search the user’s Notion workspace using the Notion MCP server and Notion Workspace Skill.
- Notion:tasks:build: Build a task from a Notion page URL
- Notion:tasks:explain-diff: Makes a Notion doc explaining a code change.
- Notion:tasks:plan: Plan a task from a Notion page URL
- Notion:tasks:setup: Set up a Notion task board for tracking tasks
- example-skills:algorithmic-art: Creating algorithmic art using p5.js with seeded randomness and interactive parameter exploration. Use this when users request creating art using code, generative art, algorithmic art, flow fields, or particle systems. Create original algorithmic art rather than copying existing artists' work to avoid copyright violations.
- example-skills:brand-guidelines: Applies Anthropic's official brand colors and typography to any sort of artifact that may benefit from having Anthropic's look-and-feel. Use it when brand colors or style guidelines, visual formatting, or company design standards apply.
- example-skills:canvas-design: Create beautiful visual art in .png and .pdf documents using design philosophy. You should use this skill when the user asks to create a poster, piece of art, design, or other static piece. Create original visual designs, never copying existing artists' work to avoid copyright violations.
- example-skills:doc-coauthoring: Guide users through a structured workflow for co-authoring documentation. Use when user wants to write documentation, proposals, technical specs, decision docs, or similar structured content. This workflow helps users efficiently transfer context, refine content through iteration, and verify the doc works for readers. Trigger when user mentions writing docs, creating proposals, drafting specs, or similar documentation tasks.
- example-skills:frontend-design: Guidance for distinctive, intentional visual design when building new UI or reshaping an existing one. Helps with aesthetic direction, typography, and making choices that don't read as templated defaults.
- example-skills:internal-comms: A set of resources to help me write all kinds of internal communications, using the formats that my company likes to use. Claude should use this skill whenever asked to write some sort of internal communications (status reports, leadership updates, 3P updates, company newsletters, FAQs, incident reports, project updates, etc.).
- example-skills:mcp-builder: Guide for creating high-quality MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers that enable LLMs to interact with external services through well-designed tools. Use when building MCP servers to integrate external APIs or services, whether in Python (FastMCP) or Node/TypeScript (MCP SDK).
- example-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- example-skills:slack-gif-creator: Knowledge and utilities for creating animated GIFs optimized for Slack. Provides constraints, validation tools, and animation concepts. Use when users request animated GIFs for Slack like "make me a GIF of X doing Y for Slack."
- example-skills:theme-factory: Toolkit for styling artifacts with a theme. These artifacts can be slides, docs, reportings, HTML landing pages, etc. There are 10 pre-set themes with colors/fonts that you can apply to any artifact that has been creating, or can generate a new theme on-the-fly.
- example-skills:web-artifacts-builder: Suite of tools for creating elaborate, multi-component claude.ai HTML artifacts using modern frontend web technologies (React, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui). Use for complex artifacts requiring state management, routing, or shadcn/ui components - not for simple single-file HTML/JSX artifacts.
- example-skills:webapp-testing: Toolkit for interacting with and testing local web applications using Playwright. Supports verifying frontend functionality, debugging UI behavior, capturing browser screenshots, and viewing browser logs.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". - fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). - schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. 1	# Quiet Library
2	
3	Quiet Library is a personal, distraction-free YouTube video library for Android. It stores only videos you deliberately save, organizes them into local folders, and plays a selected video in a constrained embedded player without exposing search, comments, Shorts, trending pages, or a general YouTube feed.
4	
5	The app targets Expo SDK 57, React Native 0.86, TypeScript, Android 14+, and the Samsung Galaxy A15.
6	
7	## What is implemented
8	
9	- Paste standard, short, mobile, music, live, embed, or Shorts-form YouTube video URLs.
10	- Validate links, reject unsupported URLs, and prevent duplicate saved videos.
11	- Load title, thumbnail, and channel through YouTube oEmbed without an API key.
12	- Enrich duration, publication date, and description through YouTube Data API v3 when a key is configured.
13	- Store saved videos, metadata, folders, assignments, and local-availability state in SQLite.
14	- Create, rename, and delete folders; move videos between folders; view all or unfiled videos.
15	- Select multiple saved videos, including all videos in the current view, then move or delete them together.
16	- Show each saved video's local availability and the queued, transferring, completed, failed, or interrupted transfer state.
17	- Download a saved video's progressive MP4 stream fully on-device into private app storage, with live progress, retry after failure or interruption, and removal of the local copy.
18	- Mark downloaded videos in every video list and provide a dedicated **Downloaded** library filter.
19	- Keep videos when deleting a folder by default, with a separate explicit destructive option.
20	- Present source-controlled channels as folder-like entries, with separate paginated Videos and Playlists views.
21	- Load additional channel, playlist, and playlist-video pages automatically near the end of each list while caching channel videos locally.
22	- Register separate Android URL intent filters for `youtu.be`, `/watch`, `/shorts`, and `/live` links so supported links can open directly in Quiet Library from the system chooser.
23	- Play only the selected video in an embedded YouTube player, block top-level YouTube navigation, and replace the player with a native replay panel at playback end instead of leaving recommendations visible.
24	- Play completed downloads directly from their private local file with `expo-video`; the YouTube player and metadata request are not loaded for local playback.
25	- Offer **Save video** in the player when a link opened from another Android app is not yet in the library.
26	- Use a dark, low-glare interface throughout the app.
27	- Show explicit loading, empty, invalid-link, API, and playback states.
28	- Use disk-backed thumbnail caching and virtualized lists for low memory use.
29	
30	## Local availability state
31	
32	Each saved video has an **Offline availability** sheet. SQLite stores its transfer state, progress, and completed local file URI. The supported states are `unavailable`, `queued`, `downloading`, `downloaded`, `failed`, and `interrupted`.
33	
34	Downloads run entirely on the device — no companion server, API key, or extra configuration is required. Stream URLs are resolved by [NewPipe Extractor](https://github.com/TeamNewPipe/NewPipeExtractor), embedded as a local Expo native module in [`modules/newpipe`](modules/newpipe); the extractor handles YouTube's client and anti-bot logic, which a bare internal-API request does not. The app then transfers the progressive MP4 into its private storage (`downloads/<videoId>.mp4`) with `expo-file-system`, updating status and progress in SQLite along the way. Because the extractor is a native Android library, downloads require a development or release build — they do not work in Expo Go.
35	
36	Notes and limitations:
37	
38	- Progressive MP4 streams carry muxed audio and video, so no on-device transcoding is needed. They typically top out at 360p (sometimes 720p); higher resolutions are only published as separate audio/video streams, which this app intentionally does not merge.
39	- Videos that are private, members-only, age-restricted, or region-locked report a reason in the Offline availability sheet and are not downloaded.
40	- Downloads that were in flight when the app closed are marked `interrupted` on the next launch and can be retried from the sheet.
41	- Removing a local copy or deleting a saved video also deletes its file from app storage.
42	- Only download videos you have the right to save offline.
43	
44	## Architecture and storage
45	
46	The app intentionally avoids a large state-management or navigation dependency.
47	
48	- `LibraryProvider` is the single application-state boundary. It coordinates repository operations, YouTube metadata, cached channel feeds, and refresh state.
49	- `NavigationProvider` is a small stack navigator with Android hardware-back handling.
50	- `expo-sqlite` stores relational local data in `quiet-library.db`. SQLite is a better fit than one large JSON value because uniqueness, folder relationships, transactions, and future migrations remain explicit and reliable. WAL mode keeps reads responsive while writes occur.
51	- `expo-image` uses memory-and-disk caching for thumbnails. Images are not copied into SQLite.
52	- `expo-video` plays completed downloads directly from their private `file://` URI.
53	- `react-native-webview` hosts the supported YouTube IFrame Player. The containing document uses the Android application ID as its HTTPS origin so YouTube receives app identity/referrer information.
54	- No background polling or background tasks are registered.
55	
56	The SQLite schema is created in [`src/data/database.ts`](src/data/database.ts). Deleting the Android app also deletes its private database and cached thumbnails.
57

115	## Prerequisites
116	
117	- Node.js 22 and npm 10
118	- Java 17
119	- Android SDK Platform 36 and Android Build Tools 36
120	- Android SDK Platform Tools (`adb`)
121	- An Expo account only if using EAS cloud builds
122	
123	Confirm the tools:
124	
125	```powershell
126	node --version
127	npm --version
128	java -version
129	adb version
130	```
131	
132	Set `ANDROID_HOME` if Android Studio did not configure it:
133	
134	```powershell
135	$env:ANDROID_HOME = "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Android\Sdk"
136	$env:Path += ";$env:ANDROID_HOME\platform-tools"
137	```
138	
139	## Install and configure
140	
141	```powershell
142	npm install
143	Copy-Item .env.example .env
144	```
145	
146	Edit `.env`:
147	
148	```dotenv
149	EXPO_PUBLIC_YOUTUBE_API_KEY=your_restricted_key
150	```
151	
152	Metadata for individually pasted videos works without this key, but durations may be unavailable. The hardcoded Channels section requires it.
153	
154	To create a key:
155

# Quiet Library

Quiet Library is a personal, distraction-free YouTube video library for Android. It stores only videos you deliberately save, organizes them into local folders, and plays a selected video in a constrained embedded player without exposing search, comments, Shorts, trending pages, or a general YouTube feed.

The app targets Expo SDK 57, React Native 0.86, TypeScript, Android 14+, and the Samsung Galaxy A15.

## What is implemented

- Paste standard, short, mobile, music, live, embed, or Shorts-form YouTube video URLs.
- Validate links, reject unsupported URLs, and prevent duplicate saved videos.
- Load title, thumbnail, and channel through YouTube oEmbed without an API key.
- Enrich duration, publication date, and description through YouTube Data API v3 when a key is configured.
- Store saved videos, metadata, folders, assignments, and local-availability state in SQLite.
- Create, rename, and delete folders; move videos between folders; view all or unfiled videos.
- Select multiple saved videos, including all videos in the current view, then move or delete them together.
- Show each saved video's local availability and the queued, transferring, completed, failed, or interrupted transfer state.
- Download a saved video's progressive MP4 stream fully on-device into private app storage, with live progress, retry after failure or interruption, and removal of the local copy.
- Mark downloaded videos in every video list and provide a dedicated **Downloaded** library filter.
- Keep videos when deleting a folder by default, with a separate explicit destructive option.
- Present source-controlled channels as folder-like entries, with separate paginated Videos and Playlists views.
- Load additional channel, playlist, and playlist-video pages automatically near the end of each list while caching channel videos locally.
- Register separate Android URL intent filters for `youtu.be`, `/watch`, `/shorts`, and `/live` links so supported links can open directly in Quiet Library from the system chooser.
- Play only the selected video in an embedded YouTube player, block top-level YouTube navigation, and replace the player with a native replay panel at playback end instead of leaving recommendations visible.
- Play completed downloads directly from their private local file with `expo-video`; the YouTube player and metadata request are not loaded for local playback.
- Offer **Save video** in the player when a link opened from another Android app is not yet in the library.
- Use a dark, low-glare interface throughout the app.
- Show explicit loading, empty, invalid-link, API, and playback states.
- Use disk-backed thumbnail caching and virtualized lists for low memory use.

## Local availability state

Each saved video has an **Offline availability** sheet. SQLite stores its transfer state, progress, and completed local file URI. The supported states are `unavailable`, `queued`, `downloading`, `downloaded`, `failed`, and `interrupted`.

Downloads run entirely on the device — no companion server, API key, or extra configuration is required. Stream URLs are resolved by [NewPipe Extractor](https://github.com/TeamNewPipe/NewPipeExtractor), embedded as a local Expo native module in [`modules/newpipe`](modules/newpipe); the extractor handles YouTube's client and anti-bot logic, which a bare internal-API request does not. The app then transfers the progressive MP4 into its private storage (`downloads/<videoId>.mp4`) with `expo-file-system`, updating status and progress in SQLite along the way. Because the extractor is a native Android library, downloads require a development or release build — they do not work in Expo Go.

Notes and limitations:

- Progressive MP4 streams carry muxed audio and video, so no on-device transcoding is needed. They typically top out at 360p (sometimes 720p); higher resolutions are only published as separate audio/video streams, which this app intentionally does not merge.
- Videos that are private, members-only, age-restricted, or region-locked report a reason in the Offline availability sheet and are not downloaded.
- Downloads that were in flight when the app closed are marked `interrupted` on the next launch and can be retried from the sheet.
- Removing a local copy or deleting a saved video also deletes its file from app storage.
- Only download videos you have the right to save offline.

## Architecture and storage

The app intentionally avoids a large state-management or navigation dependency.

- `LibraryProvider` is the single application-state boundary. It coordinates repository operations, YouTube metadata, cached channel feeds, and refresh state.
- `NavigationProvider` is a small stack navigator with Android hardware-back handling.
- `expo-sqlite` stores relational local data in `quiet-library.db`. SQLite is a better fit than one large JSON value because uniqueness, folder relationships, transactions, and future migrations remain explicit and reliable. WAL mode keeps reads responsive while writes occur.
- `expo-image` uses memory-and-disk caching for thumbnails. Images are not copied into SQLite.
- `expo-video` plays completed downloads directly from their private `file://` URI.
- `react-native-webview` hosts the supported YouTube IFrame Player. The containing document uses the Android application ID as its HTTPS origin so YouTube receives app identity/referrer information.
- No background polling or background tasks are registered.

The SQLite schema is created in [`src/data/database.ts`](src/data/database.ts). Deleting the Android app also deletes its private database and cached thumbnails.

## Prerequisites

lines: Downloads run entirely on the device — no companion server, API key, or extra configuration is required. Stream URLs are resolved by [NewPipe Extractor](https://github.com/TeamNewPipe/NewPipeExtractor), embedded as a local Expo native module in [`modules/newpipe`](modules/newpipe); the extractor handles YouTube's client and anti-bot logic, which a bare internal-API request does not. The app then transfers the progressive MP4 into its private storage (`downloads/<videoId>.mp4`) with `expo-file-system`, updating status and progress in SQLite along the way. Because the extractor is a native Android library, downloads require a development or release build — they do not work in Expo Go.

### Schema migrations and your existing data

Migrations are versioned with `PRAGMA user_version` and run once on startup. Every step from version 4 onward is additive — `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` and `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` only — so upgrading never rewrites or drops a table that holds saved videos, folders, notes, or download state. Reinstalling with `adb install -r` keeps the app's private storage, which is where both `quiet-library.db` and the downloaded media files live, as long as the APK signature does not change.

Version 5 adds: `saved_videos.notes`, `saved_videos.download_kind`, `folders.parent_id` (subfolders), `channel_videos.position` (stable ordering), and the `channel_playlists`, `playlist_videos`, and `paging_state` tables.

### Exporting

**Folders → share icon** writes `quiet-library-<timestamp>.json` into the app cache and opens the Android share sheet. The file contains every folder (with its parent), every saved video with its canonical URL, metadata, notes, folder assignment, and whether a local copy exists. Media files themselves are not included.

content.text:
Everything is built, installed, and running on your device. Here's the state of each item:

**Downloads**
- **3-dot menu** now starts a download directly — *Download video* or *Download audio only* — plus *Remove local copy* when one exists. "Offline availability" is still there.
- **Audio downloads** save the best M4A/AAC track YouTube publishes and play in a compact audio player (seek bar, ±15s, elapsed/total time). I did **not** name it MP3: real MP3 would need FFmpeg bundled into the app just to re-encode, and every Android app plays M4A natively.
- **Multi-select → download** works in Saved, inside a folder, and inside a channel (channel videos get saved to a folder you pick first, then downloaded). Each asks video-or-audio.
- **Download-all icon** sits in the folder header and in the Saved toolbar; it grabs everything shown that isn't already on the device. All downloads run through a **one-at-a-time queue**, so selecting 40 videos doesn't open 40 transfers.

**The scrolling bug** — root cause found: every time you re-entered a channel, the app refetched page 1 and *deleted* the cached rows for that channel, so 200 loaded videos collapsed back to 20 and the list jumped to the top. Now the cache is only replaced when you explicitly hit Refresh. The pagination cursor and scroll position are both remembered, and a `position` column keeps the order stable instead of re-sorting by date.

**Also done:** channel multi-select (with bulk refresh) · search inside a channel, inside Saved, inside a folder, and inside playlists · Shorts hidden from channel lists (≤62s or `#shorts`) · publication age + duration on every card, with a one-time backfill for old entries that were missing it · per-video notes saved as you type · playlists and their videos cached in SQLite · "New folder" (and per-folder "+" for subfolders) inside every save sheet · subfolders with a nested Folders screen, indented pickers, and parent filters that include children · JSON export via the share icon on Folders · screen stays awake on the player · background playback with a media notification.

**Two things to know:**
- Background playback covers **downloaded** video and audio. Streamed YouTube playback runs in a WebView and stops when backgrounded — that one isn't fixable without violating YouTube's embed terms.
- Deleting a folder now lifts its subfolders up one level instead of orphaning them.

**Your data is intact** — the reinstall used the same signing key and every migration is additive (`ADD COLUMN` / `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` only). The screenshot after launch showed all **25 videos** and your **Mind / PHT / Workout** folders, with no crash in logcat.

What I couldn't verify from here is the runtime behavior of an actual audio download, background playback, and the export share sheet — those need taps, and you picked the phone up while I was checking. If any of them misbehaves, tell me what you see and I'll trace it.

content.text:
All four fixes are built, installed, and running (v1.3.0, versionCode 5).

1. **Chip padding** — verified on screen. The filter row now has a proper gap below it instead of the cards butting up against it.
2. **Channel search now queries YouTube.** Cached matches still appear instantly, then results from `search.list` scoped to that channel get appended below them (deduped, Shorts filtered, scrolling loads more pages). It waits 650 ms after you stop typing and needs 2+ characters, because that call costs 100 quota units against your 10k/day — so a typed phrase costs one search, not one per keystroke. A "Searching *channel*…" line shows while it runs.
3. **Back from a channel returns to the Channels tab.** The cause was `HomeScreen` holding the tab in local state that reset to "Saved" every time the screen remounted; the choice now survives the round trip.
4. **Notes field lifts above the keyboard.** On focus, the scroll view adds bottom room and scrolls the field to the top of the visible area once the keyboard has resized the window.

Two things I noticed while checking:

- **Your downloads are working** — "Lying Paused Rope Face Pull" and "Escape the cave" both show **Downloaded** now. That 0% badge I flagged last time was just a transfer in progress, not a stuck row.
- Playlist caching is live too: the Better Ideas → Playlists tab loaded "My favorite videos · 15".

I verified fix 1 visually and confirmed the app launches clean with your 27 videos intact. I stopped short of driving the UI for fixes 2–4 because you were on the phone at the same time — one of my verification taps switched Better Ideas over to its Playlists tab, so if that jumped under you, that was me.

content.text:
All four are fixed and installed. Your session actually verified the most important one for me — more on that below.

**1. Filter chips.** The chips weren't just tight, they were a fixed row that cards scrolled *underneath*, so the top card got sliced mid-title. Adding padding couldn't fix that. The search field and chip row are now part of the scrolling content, so they move up with the list and nothing can be drawn over a card.

**2. Parallel downloads.** The queue now runs **3 transfers at once** instead of strictly one at a time; anything beyond that waits, so selecting a whole folder still can't open dozens of connections.

**3. Audio slowness — root cause found.** It wasn't the file size. YouTube serves *adaptive* streams (all audio-only tracks) at roughly playback speed when you fetch them in a single request; the progressive MP4 URLs the video path uses carry a `ratebypass` flag and aren't paced that way. So a 10 MB audio file crawled while a 40 MB video flew.

The fix is what yt-dlp and the NewPipe app both do: request the file in explicit **4 MB byte ranges**, which each transfer at full line speed. I moved the whole transfer into the native module (OkHttp, 4 download threads) rather than `expo-file-system`, so the bytes never cross into JavaScript and progress arrives as native events.

**4. Cache reset — this was a real bug, not you mis-tapping.** Refresh (both the channel header button and the Channels-tab bulk refresh) did `DELETE` all cached rows for that channel and re-insert only page 1. That's exactly the 100 → 20 collapse. Every cache write is now a merge — nothing is ever deleted, and the list is ordered by publication date, so a refresh only adds newer uploads on top of everything you've already scrolled through.

**What your own session confirmed:** while I was checking the new build, "STRAIGHT-BAR LAT PRAYER" finished as **🎵 Audio** and "How To Cure Brain Fog" was mid-transfer at **38%**. That's the new native ranged downloader running end to end — resolve, chunked transfer, live progress, completion. Whether it *feels* faster now is your call to make; the throttling mechanism it works around is well documented, but I have no before/after timing of my own.

I stopped driving the UI once it was clear you were using the phone — one stray tap of mine landed on your list around 2:22, which is why nothing opened.
